claim: The 185-odorant panel covers a wide range of odorant chemical space as defined by physicochemical descriptors taken from a list of compounds curated for use in flavors and fragrances.
source: The panel covered a wide range of odorant chemical space as defined by physicochemical descriptors taken from a list of compounds curated for use in flavors and fragrances (Figure 1A; Pashkovski et al., 2020) (see Materials and methods), and included a diversity of chemical classes as defined by functional group and other structural features (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the coverage of physicochemical space, citation to Pashkovski et al., 2020, and reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: Odorant concentrations were systematically adjusted across a >1000 fold (sub-picomolar to nanomolar) range to identify high-sensitivity odorant-glomerulus interactions.
source: Rather than deliver odorants at a single arbitrarily- or empirically-chosen concentration, we used a rational search strategy that allowed adjusting the concentration of each odorant across a >1000 fold (sub-pico- to nanomolar) range in order to identify high-sensitivity odorant-glomerulus interactions and to, ideally, pair each glomerulus with its primary odorant.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the experimental approach.

claim: Mouse perceptual thresholds are in the picomolar range for at least some odorants.
source: Guided by recent studies indicating mouse perceptual thresholds in the picomolar range for at least some odorants (Dewan et al., 2018; Williams and Dewan, 2020), we initially set estimated delivered odorant concentrations to ~1 pM (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dewan et al., 2018 and Williams and Dewan, 2020.

claim: Initial estimated delivered odorant concentrations were set to approximately 1 pM.
source: Guided by recent studies indicating mouse perceptual thresholds in the picomolar range for at least some odorants (Dewan et al., 2018; Williams and Dewan, 2020), we initially set estimated delivered odorant concentrations to ~1 pM (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the experimental protocol.

claim: Concentrations were systematically increased or decreased by tenfold steps up to approximately 1 nM to identify the lowest concentration for each odorant capable of reliably activating at least one glomerulus.
source: Across a series of pilot experiments, concentrations were then systematically increased (or occasionally decreased) by tenfold steps up to ~1 nM to identify the lowest concentration for each odorant capable of reliably activating at least one glomerulus, with responses averaged across at least three trials (typically, four) per concentration and odorant.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the experimental procedure.

claim: Final analyzed concentrations were identical across animals for the majority of odorants (145/185).
source: Final analyzed concentrations were identical across animals for the majority of odorants (145/185), and none differed by more than tenfold across the four mice.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: No odorant concentration differed by more than tenfold across the four mice.
source: Final analyzed concentrations were identical across animals for the majority of odorants (145/185), and none differed by more than tenfold across the four mice.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: 163 of 185 odorants (88%) evoked responses in one or more dorsal glomeruli per OB per mouse.
source: Nearly all odorants tested proved effective within the picomolar-to-nanomolar concentration range: 163 of 185 odorants (88%) evoked responses in one or more dorsal glomeruli per OB per mouse, and only twelve odorants proved ineffective (i.e. failed to elicit a response in any OB).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data from the experiments.

claim: Only twelve odorants failed to elicit a response in any OB.
source: Nearly all odorants tested proved effective within the picomolar-to-nanomolar concentration range: 163 of 185 odorants (88%) evoked responses in one or more dorsal glomeruli per OB per mouse, and only twelve odorants proved ineffective (i.e. failed to elicit a response in any OB).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data from the experiments.

claim: Response amplitudes were lognormally distributed.
source: Response amplitudes were lognormally distributed (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), with a mean ln(∆F/F) of 1.48 (corresponding to 4.4% ∆F/F, mean of means across 8 OBs; mean s.d. of responses: 1.03 ln(∆F/F); number of responses per OB: 308–484).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) and specific numerical data.

claim: The mean ln(∆F/F) of response amplitudes was 1.48, corresponding to 4.4% ∆F/F.
source: Response amplitudes were lognormally distributed (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), with a mean ln(∆F/F) of 1.48 (corresponding to 4.4% ∆F/F, mean of means across 8 OBs; mean s.d. of responses: 1.03 ln(∆F/F); number of responses per OB: 308–484).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data from the experiments.

claim: Patterns of glomerular activation were remarkably consistent across all eight OBs.
source: Qualitatively, patterns of glomerular activation were remarkably consistent across all eight OBs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a qualitative observation from the data.

claim: There were only modest differences in overall response magnitudes across mice or between left and right OBs in the same mouse.
source: There were only modest differences in overall response magnitudes across mice or between left and right OBs in the same mouse (ANOVA on all nonzero ∆F/F responses for each OB (F7,3385=12.97, p<2e–16); post-hoc Tukey's multiple comparisons of means: p=7e–7 for 1 of 4 left vs. right OB pairs; p>0.5 for 3 of 4 pairs); these differences likely reflect differences in nasal patency between mice or between sides.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA and post-hoc tests) with specific p-values.

claim: Differences in response magnitudes likely reflect differences in nasal patency between mice or between sides.
source: There were only modest differences in overall response magnitudes across mice or between left and right OBs in the same mouse (ANOVA on all nonzero ∆F/F responses for each OB (F7,3385=12.97, p<2e–16); post-hoc Tukey's multiple comparisons of means: p=7e–7 for 1 of 4 left vs. right OB pairs; p>0.5 for 3 of 4 pairs); these differences likely reflect differences in nasal patency between mice or between sides.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the observed data.

claim: The cumulative number of glomeruli activated across the odorant panel ranged from 103 to 142 per OB with a median of 126.
source: The cumulative number of glomeruli activated across the odorant panel ranged from 103 to 142 per OB (median: 126) and covered the extent of the dorsal OB (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A recent report mapping ORs to the OB identified approximately 130 ORs/TAARs from the same area of the OB imaged in the present study.
source: A recent report mapping ORs to the OB identified ~130 ORs/trace amine-associated receptors (TAARs) from the same area of the OB imaged in the present study (Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2021.

claim: A range of 150–160 glomeruli is a reasonable estimate of the number of glomeruli present in the imaging area.
source: Allowing for failure to detect low-abundance ORs in Zhu et al., 2021 and slight mismatches in tissue area, a range of 150–160 glomeruli is a reasonable estimate of the number of glomeruli present in our imaging area.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference based on data from Zhu et al., 2021 and considerations of detection limitations.

claim: The odorant panel was able to identify 75–90% of glomeruli in the imaged area.
source: Thus we estimate that our odorant panel was able to identify 75–90% of glomeruli in the imaged area.
evidence: The claim is stated as an estimate based on the number of activated glomeruli and the estimated total number of glomeruli.

claim: Final estimated concentrations ranged from 4 × 10–14 to 4 × 10–9 M with a median of 1 × 10–10 M (2.4 ppb).
source: Across all odorants, final estimated concentrations ranged from 4 × 10–14 to 4 × 10–9 M (median: 1 × 10–10 M, 2.4 ppb) (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Maximal glomerular sensitivity had a median concentration of 2 × 10–11 M (0.5 ppb).
source: Maximal glomerular sensitivity (i.e. the concentration at which each glomerulus responded to its primary odorant) was distributed across even lower concentrations, with a median of 2 × 10–11 M (0.5 ppb) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: The concentrations used are substantially lower than those used to characterize odorant representations in earlier studies, by as much as 4–5 orders of magnitude.
source: These concentrations are, overall, substantially lower than those used to characterize odorant representations in earlier studies, by as much as 4–5 orders of magnitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and indicate that high odorant sensitivity is a general feature of OSN inputs to glomeruli.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2 comparing concentrations across studies.

claim: High odorant sensitivity is a general feature of OSN inputs to glomeruli.
source: These concentrations are, overall, substantially lower than those used to characterize odorant representations in earlier studies, by as much as 4–5 orders of magnitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and indicate that high odorant sensitivity is a general feature of OSN inputs to glomeruli.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the concentration data.

claim: Each effective odorant evoked input to only a few glomeruli with a median of 2 glomeruli per odorant.
source: Our experimental approach was designed to yield sparse glomerular responses to each odorant. Nevertheless, the degree of sparseness was striking, with each effective odorant evoking input to only a few glomeruli (median: 2 glomeruli per odorant; quartiles: 1–3 glomeruli per odorant; 1290 responses across 8 OBs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Population sparseness was exceptionally high with a median SP of 0.994.
source: Population sparseness (SP), a measure of the selectivity of glomerular activation for a given odorant, was exceptionally high (median SP: 0.994; quartiles: 0.990–0.997, calculated from mean SP per odorant across 8 OBs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: There was no difference in SP between the left and right OBs of the same mouse.
source: There was no difference in SP between the left and right OBs of the same mouse (paired Wilcoxon Signed-Ranks test, Bonferroni-corrected p-values for each of 4 mice: p=0.12, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing with specific p-values.

claim: Individual glomeruli are narrowly tuned across the entire odorant panel.
source: This result implies that individual glomeruli are narrowly tuned across the entire odorant panel.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the high population sparseness data.

claim: Earlier characterizations of OR tuning have identified a mix of narrowly- and broadly-tuned ORs.
source: Earlier characterizations of OR tuning have identified a mix of narrowly- and broadly-tuned ORs (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Saito et al., 2009; Nara et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Saito et al., 2009; and Nara et al., 2011.

claim: Narrow tuning of OSN inputs to nearly all glomeruli was observed.
source: Here, we observed narrow tuning of OSN inputs to nearly all glomeruli, and for glomeruli tuned to nearly all odorants (Figure 1E and F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 1E, F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Lifetime sparseness was extremely high across the glomerular population with a median value of 0.995.
source: Lifetime sparseness (SL), a measure of stimulus selectivity that reflects the distribution of response magnitudes across a stimulus set and ranges from 0 (no stimulus selectivity) to 1 (response to only a single stimulus) (Davison and Katz, 2007; Schlief and Wilson, 2007), was extremely high across the glomerular population, with a median value of 0.995 (mean of medians across 8 OBs; mean quartiles: 0.989–1) (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data, supported by Figure 1H, and references definitions from Davison and Katz, 2007 and Schlief and Wilson, 2007.

claim: 25–30% of glomeruli in a given OB responded to only one odorant from the panel.
source: 25–30% of glomeruli in a given OB (mean ± s.d.: 29% ± 6%, 288/1004 total glomeruli) responded to only one odorant from the panel, and only 19% of glomeruli (187/1004) responded to more than five odorants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Only 19% of glomeruli responded to more than five odorants.
source: 25–30% of glomeruli in a given OB (mean ± s.d.: 29% ± 6%, 288/1004 total glomeruli) responded to only one odorant from the panel, and only 19% of glomeruli (187/1004) responded to more than five odorants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Sparse responses and narrow tuning of glomeruli was not due to an 'iceberg effect' where only a few odorants evoked responses detectable above the signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Sparse responses and narrow tuning of glomeruli was not due to an 'iceberg effect', in which only a few odorants evoked responses detectable above the signal-to-noise ratio of our imaging approach, as response amplitudes were typically many times greater than baseline variance levels.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the observation that response amplitudes were much greater than baseline variance.

claim: 75% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant had a dynamic range greater than 2.
source: 75% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant (n=716) had a dynamic range (i.e. the ratio between the strongest and weakest odorant responses) greater than 2, 50% had a range greater than 4, and 20% had a range greater than 10, indicating a high dynamic range in odorant responsiveness even in this low-concentration regime.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: 50% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant had a dynamic range greater than 4.
source: 75% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant (n=716) had a dynamic range (i.e. the ratio between the strongest and weakest odorant responses) greater than 2, 50% had a range greater than 4, and 20% had a range greater than 10, indicating a high dynamic range in odorant responsiveness even in this low-concentration regime.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: 20% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant had a dynamic range greater than 10.
source: 75% of glomeruli that responded to more than one odorant (n=716) had a dynamic range (i.e. the ratio between the strongest and weakest odorant responses) greater than 2, 50% had a range greater than 4, and 20% had a range greater than 10, indicating a high dynamic range in odorant responsiveness even in this low-concentration regime.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: SL values were consistently high and independent of both dynamic range and maximum response amplitude.
source: SL values were also consistently high and independent of both dynamic range and maximum response amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, E), indicating that sparse responses are not an artifact of low signal-to-noise ratios or of weakly-responding glomeruli.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3D and E.

claim: Sparse responses are not an artifact of low signal-to-noise ratios or of weakly-responding glomeruli.
source: SL values were also consistently high and independent of both dynamic range and maximum response amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, E), indicating that sparse responses are not an artifact of low signal-to-noise ratios or of weakly-responding glomeruli.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the independence of SL values from dynamic range and response amplitude.

claim: 159 odorants of the panel were presented at tenfold higher concentrations in two separate preparations using two-photon imaging.
source: We further tested the concentration-dependence of OSN tuning by presenting 159 odorants of the panel at tenfold higher concentrations in two separate preparations (the remaining 26 odorants were presented at the same concentration as the widefield imaging set but omitted from this concentration-dependent analysis; see Supplementary file 1), using two-photon imaging from a central subregion of the dorsal OB in order to more precisely attribute signals to specific glomeruli (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Glomerular tuning was only slightly broader at tenfold higher concentrations, with 12% of glomeruli activated by only one of the 159 odorants and a median SL of 0.983.
source: Glomerular tuning was only slightly broader at these higher concentrations, with 12% of glomeruli activated by only one of the 159 odorants and a median SL of 0.983 (quartiles: 0.973–0.994; 100 responsive glomeruli, 2 mice) (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1G and H.

claim: Narrow OSN tuning was not restricted to carefully-chosen perithreshold concentrations.
source: Narrow OSN tuning was thus not restricted to carefully-chosen perithreshold concentrations, suggesting that sparse and selective glomerular activation is a robust feature of odorant representations in low-concentration regimes.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the observation of narrow tuning at higher concentrations.

claim: Sparse and selective glomerular activation is a robust feature of odorant representations in low-concentration regimes.
source: Narrow OSN tuning was thus not restricted to carefully-chosen perithreshold concentrations, suggesting that sparse and selective glomerular activation is a robust feature of odorant representations in low-concentration regimes.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the concentration-dependence data.

claim: Previous studies examining neural responses to higher concentrations have proposed that odorant identity can be reliably encoded within a structured, lower-dimensional neural coding space.
source: Previous studies examining neural responses to higher concentrations have proposed that odorant identity can be reliably encoded within a structured, lower-dimensional neural coding space (Chae et al., 2019; Si et al., 2019; Pashkovski et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chae et al., 2019; Si et al., 2019; and Pashkovski et al., 2020.

claim: Glomerulus-odorant response matrices in the low-concentration datasets appeared high-dimensional.
source: However, glomerulus-odorant response matrices in our low-concentration datasets appeared high-dimensional, at least in the Euclidean domain.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The first principal component in each OB dataset accounted for only 4–7% of the total variance.
source: The first principal component (PC) in each OB dataset accounted for only 4–7% of the total variance (Figure 1I), and 54–67 PCs (44–55% of possible PCs, given 100–140 glomeruli per OB) were required to account for 90% of the response variance (Figure 1J), with similar results observed for the tenfold higher concentration two-photon dataset.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1I.

claim: 54–67 PCs (44–55% of possible PCs) were required to account for 90% of the response variance.
source: The first principal component (PC) in each OB dataset accounted for only 4–7% of the total variance (Figure 1I), and 54–67 PCs (44–55% of possible PCs, given 100–140 glomeruli per OB) were required to account for 90% of the response variance (Figure 1J), with similar results observed for the tenfold higher concentration two-photon dataset.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by Figure 1J.

claim: A comparable analysis of glomerular responses to substantially higher odorant concentrations required 21 PCs to account for 90% of the response variance in a pseudopopulation of 871 glomeruli.
source: These results substantially differ from the 21 PCs required to account for 90% of the response variance in a pseudopopulation of 871 glomeruli (i.e. ~2.4% of possible PCs) in a comparable analysis of glomerular responses to substantially higher odorant concentrations (Chae et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chae et al., 2019.

claim: Effective dimensionality was substantially higher in the main dataset (mean ± s.d.: 48.6±4.4, n=8 OBs) than that reported for odorant responses imaged from OB projections to piriform cortex using higher odorant concentrations (ED: 13.5).
source: Effective dimensionality (ED), a measure of response covariance across a dataset (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017), was also substantially higher in our main dataset (mean ± s.d.: 48.6±4.4, n=8 OBs) than that reported for odorant responses imaged from OB projections to piriform cortex using higher odorant concentrations (ED: 13.5, n=22 odorants x 3160 axonal boutons) (Pashkovski et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and supported by citations to Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017 and Pashkovski et al., 2020.

claim: A publicly available dataset describing OSN inputs to mouse OB glomeruli was collected using near-identical imaging methods and the same OMP-IRES-tTA driver line as in the present study, but with a less-sensitive GCaMP2 reporter and higher odorant concentrations.
source: To that end, we took advantage of a publicly available dataset describing OSN inputs to mouse OB glomeruli, collected using near-identical imaging methods and the same OMP-IRES-tTA driver line as in the present study, but with a less-sensitive GCaMP2 reporter and higher odorant concentrations (Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2012.

claim: The median concentration in the Ma et al., 2012 dataset was 4.3 ppm, approximately 1000x higher than in the current dataset (median: 3.4 ppb).
source: We generated response matrices using the lowest effective concentrations reported in this previous study for the 31 odorants common with the current study (median: 4.3 ppm; quartiles: 1.0–15.1 ppm), which were approximately 1000 x higher than in our dataset (median: 3.4 ppb; quartiles: 0.5–25 ppb) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and reference to Supplementary file 3.

claim: Odorants in the higher-concentration regime activated substantially more glomeruli across the same area of the dorsal OB, with a quartile range of 2–23 glomeruli per odorant (median: 5) compared to a range of 1.4–2.9 in the current dataset (median: 1.75).
source: As expected, odorants in this higher-concentration regime activated substantially more glomeruli across the same area of the dorsal OB, with a quartile range of 2–23 glomeruli per odorant (median: 5) compared to a range of 1.4–2.9 in our dataset (median of mean values across 8 OBs: 1.75; p=3 × 10–5, paired Wilcoxon Signed Ranks).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and statistical testing.

claim: SL of individual glomeruli across the 31 odorants was significantly lower in the higher-concentration dataset, with a quartile range of 0.84–0.97 (median: 0.9) compared to a range of 0.97–1 in the current dataset (median: 1).
source: SL of individual glomeruli across the 31 odorants was also significantly lower, with a quartile range of 0.84–0.97 (median: 0.9; n=98 glomeruli from one OB) compared to a range of 0.97–1 in our dataset (median: 1; n=273 glomeruli from 8 OBs; p=0, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and statistical testing.

claim: Dimensionality of the glomerular responses across the 31 odorant panel was substantially lower for the higher concentration data, with an ED of 5.3 compared to 13.2±1.1 (mean ± s.d., 8 OBs).
source: Dimensionality of the glomerular responses across the 31 odorant panel was also substantially lower for the higher concentration data, with an ED of 5.3 compared to 13.2±1.1 (mean ± s.d., 8 OBs).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: The narrow tuning of glomeruli and sparser, higher dimensional odorant response patterns directly reflect differences in how odorant information is represented in the much lower concentration regime, rather than differences in odorant panel composition.
source: This comparison thus further confirms that the narrow tuning of glomeruli and sparser, higher dimensional odorant response patterns in our dataset directly reflect differences in how odorant information is represented in this much lower concentration regime, rather than differences in odorant panel composition.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the comparison with the Ma et al., 2012 dataset.

claim: The narrow tuning and high sensitivity of glomeruli to their primary odorants suggests that many glomeruli can be identified simply by their response to a single diagnostic odorant delivered at low concentration.
source: The narrow tuning and high sensitivity of glomeruli to their primary odorants suggests that many glomeruli can be identified simply by their response to a single diagnostic odorant delivered at low concentration.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the narrow tuning and high sensitivity data.

claim: The aromatic ester phenyl acetate (~3 pM) strongly activated a single glomerulus in the central OB, with identical response spectra across the 8 OBs.
source: For example, the aromatic ester phenyl acetate (~3 pM) strongly activated a single glomerulus in the central OB, with identical response spectra across the 8 OBs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 2A and B.

claim: The odorant methyl tiglate (~10 pM) strongly activated a single glomerulus in the central-medial OB in each of the 8 OBs imaged.
source: Likewise, the odorant methyl tiglate (~10 pM) strongly activated a single glomerulus in the central-medial OB in each of the 8 OBs imaged; this glomerulus was also strongly- and singly-activated by ethyl, hexyl, and isopropyl tiglate, as well as trans-2-methyl-2-butenal and 2-methyl-2-pentenoic acid (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 2A and B.

claim: In many cases, a single diagnostic odorant can be used to identify putatively cognate glomeruli across animals.
source: These observations suggest that, in many cases, a single diagnostic odorant can be used to identify putatively cognate glomeruli across animals.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the observations of consistent glomerular activation.

claim: 80 odorants passed the screen for singular or near-singular glomerular activation and reliability.
source: For each of the 80 odorants passing this screen, we tested the odorant's ability to identify glomeruli across OBs by comparing the response spectrum of the glomerulus most strongly activated by that odorant across the full 185-odorant panel with that of all other glomeruli in each OB.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: For 19 odorants, the strongest activated glomerulus identified the glomerulus with the highest-correlated response spectrum in 100% of comparisons (median correlation coefficient: 0.95±0.04).
source: For 19 odorants, the strongest (or only) activated glomerulus identified the glomerulus with the highest-correlated response spectrum in 100% of comparisons (median correlation coefficient [Pearson's r] across OBs: 0.95±0.04; mean ± s.d., n=19).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: Relaxing the criteria to allow for inherent variability yielded 22 additional odorants.
source: Relaxing these criteria slightly to allow for inherent variability in responsiveness across the odorant panel – to a cutoff of 80% match between the strongest-activated and most-correlated glomerulus across OBs (error ratio <0.2; see Materials and methods) and a median correlation coefficient in response spectra of >0.8 – yielded 22 additional odorants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: 41 odorants from the original 185-odorant panel could serve as diagnostic probes to identify 26 unique glomeruli.
source: Thus, 41 odorants from the original 185-odorant panel could serve as diagnostic probes to identify 26 unique glomeruli (Table 1; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data and reference to Table 1 and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Glomeruli identified with this approach appeared in a similar location on the dorsal OB, with a spatial jitter consistent with that characterized for OR-defined OSN projections.
source: Notably, while spatial location was not used as a diagnostic criterion, glomeruli identified with this approach appeared in a similar location on the dorsal OB, with a spatial jitter consistent with that characterized for OR-defined OSN projections (Figure 2C; Table 1; Zapiec and Mombaerts, 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 2C, Table 1, and citation to Zapiec and Mombaerts, 2015.

claim: Diagnostic odorant-concentration pairs evoked singular activation of the same putatively identified glomeruli in awake, head-fixed mice at the same low concentrations.
source: Diagnostic odorant-concentration pairs also evoked singular activation of the same putatively identified glomeruli in awake, head-fixed mice at the same low concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that OSNs are similarly sensitive and selective during natural odorant sampling.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: OSNs are similarly sensitive and selective during natural odorant sampling.
source: Diagnostic odorant-concentration pairs also evoked singular activation of the same putatively identified glomeruli in awake, head-fixed mice at the same low concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that OSNs are similarly sensitive and selective during natural odorant sampling.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the observation of similar responses in awake mice.

claim: The high selectivity and sensitivity of OSNs for their primary odorants allows for simple and robust identification of cognate glomeruli across OBs using a single odorant-concentration pair.
source: Thus, the high selectivity and sensitivity of OSNs for their primary odorants allows for simple and robust identification of cognate glomeruli across OBs using a single odorant-concentration pair.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the diagnostic odorant data.

claim: Individual glomeruli are sensitively and selectively tuned to a very narrow portion of odorant chemical space.
source: By mapping high-sensitivity odorant responses to OB glomeruli using a large and diverse odorant panel, we found that individual glomeruli – and, by inference, their cognate ORs – are sensitively and selectively tuned to a very narrow portion of odorant chemical space.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary conclusion from the mapping experiments.

claim: Narrow tuning leads to a sparse and apparently high-dimensional representation of individual odorants in the regime of low odorant concentrations.
source: This narrow tuning leads to a sparse and apparently high-dimensional representation of individual odorants in the regime of low odorant concentrations.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the narrow tuning data.

claim: The small amount of structure apparent in the coding regime was well-represented by relatively simple descriptions of chemical space derived from odorant structural features.
source: At the same time, the small amount of structure that was apparent in this coding regime – both in terms of glomerular tuning and glomerular location – was well-represented by relatively simple descriptions of chemical space derived from odorant structural features.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary conclusion from the chemical descriptor analysis.

claim: The prevalence of narrowly-tuned glomeruli and the degree of selectivity in their tuning was striking.
source: The prevalence of narrowly-tuned glomeruli, and the degree of selectivity in their tuning, was striking.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Some earlier characterizations of OSN tuning have concluded that the majority of OSNs are narrowly tuned to odorants with shared structural motifs.
source: While some earlier characterizations of OSN tuning have concluded that the majority of OSNs (and, thus, the ORs they express) are narrowly tuned to odorants with shared structural motifs (Araneda et al., 2000; Nara et al., 2011) – a result qualitatively similar to that seen here – most prior studies have reported a combination of broadly- and narrowly-tuned ORs and OSNs (Sicard and Holley, 1984; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Grosmaitre et al., 2009; Saito et al., 2009; Nara et al., 2011; Del Mármol et al., 2021), with even those OSNs classified as narrowly tuned appearing less selective than the majority of glomeruli in our dataset.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Araneda et al., 2000 and Nara et al., 2011.

claim: Most prior studies have reported a combination of broadly- and narrowly-tuned ORs and OSNs.
source: While some earlier characterizations of OSN tuning have concluded that the majority of OSNs (and, thus, the ORs they express) are narrowly tuned to odorants with shared structural motifs (Araneda et al., 2000; Nara et al., 2011) – a result qualitatively similar to that seen here – most prior studies have reported a combination of broadly- and narrowly-tuned ORs and OSNs (Sicard and Holley, 1984; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Grosmaitre et al., 2009; Saito et al., 2009; Nara et al., 2011; Del Mármol et al., 2021), with even those OSNs classified as narrowly tuned appearing less selective than the majority of glomeruli in our dataset.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sicard and Holley, 1984; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Grosmaitre et al., 2009; Saito et al., 2009; Nara et al., 2011; and Del Mármol et al., 2021.

claim: Some earlier characterizations of mitral/tufted cell tuning in the mouse have indicated high odorant selectivity, but reported lifetime sparseness values substantially lower than those found in the current study.
source: Likewise, some earlier characterizations of mitral/tufted cell tuning in the mouse have indicated high odorant selectivity, but reported lifetime sparseness values across a range of odorants that are substantially lower (indicating broader tuning) than those found here (Davison and Katz, 2007; Fantana et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Davison and Katz, 2007; Fantana et al., 2008; and Tan et al., 2010.

claim: A likely explanation for the difference in tuning is the much lower range of odorant concentrations used to characterize glomerular specificity in the current study.
source: A likely explanation for this difference is the much lower range of odorant concentrations used to characterize glomerular specificity here.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference to explain differences with prior studies.

claim: Odorants were presented at concentrations several orders of magnitude lower than those in earlier in vivo studies.
source: In general, we presented odorants at concentrations several orders of magnitude lower than those in earlier in vivo studies (Rubin and Katz, 1999; Davison and Katz, 2007; Soucy et al., 2009; Ma et al., 2012; Chae et al., 2019; Pashkovski et al., 2020), and 4–6 orders of magnitude lower than in vitro studies (Saito et al., 2009; Nara et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Glomeruli remained narrowly tuned even when challenged with tenfold higher concentrations.
source: Glomeruli remained narrowly tuned even when challenged with tenfold higher concentrations, and narrow tuning was not a function of poor signal-to-noise ratios nor of the particular selection of concentrations used for each odorant.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the concentration-dependence experiments.

claim: Highly selective tuning to odorants appears to be a robust feature of OSN input to OB glomeruli.
source: Thus, highly selective tuning to odorants appears to be a robust feature of OSN input to OB glomeruli.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion drawn from the tuning data across concentrations.

claim: The high sensitivity of glomeruli to their primary odorant was surprising.
source: The high sensitivity of glomeruli to their primary odorant was also surprising: the median primary odorant concentration across all glomeruli was 2 × 10–11 M; threshold concentrations for characteristic odorant-glomerulus pairs are likely even lower, as we did not attempt to determine threshold sensitivities for any glomerulus.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: The median primary odorant concentration across all glomeruli was 2 × 10–11 M.
source: The high sensitivity of glomeruli to their primary odorant was also surprising: the median primary odorant concentration across all glomeruli was 2 × 10–11 M; threshold concentrations for characteristic odorant-glomerulus pairs are likely even lower, as we did not attempt to determine threshold sensitivities for any glomerulus.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numerical data.

claim: Threshold concentrations for characteristic odorant-glomerulus pairs are likely even lower than the median primary odorant concentration.

evidence: The claim is stated as an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: These concentrations are comparable to the sensitivity of the 'ultrasensitive' TAAR OSNs for their preferred ligands.
source: These concentrations are comparable to the sensitivity of the 'ultrasensitive' TAAR OSNs for their preferred ligands (Zhang et al., 2013), and substantially lower than those reported for other OSNs in vivo (Oka et al., 2006; Tan et al., 2010).

claim: The discrepancy in sensitivity could be explained by the smaller odorant panels used in earlier studies, resulting in a failure to find optimal odorants for a given OSN/OR.

claim: The concentrations used in the current study were comparable to or higher than psychophysical detection thresholds measured with rigorous behavioral assays in mice.
source: We note that the concentrations used here were comparable to or higher than psychophysical detection thresholds measured with rigorous behavioral assays in mice (Dewan et al., 2018; Cichy et al., 2019; Williams and Dewan, 2020), suggesting that the sparse responses at these concentrations can support odor perception.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dewan et al., 2018; Cichy et al., 2019; and Williams and Dewan, 2020.

claim: Given the low covariance in responses across the OSN population for different odorants, canonical models may be less applicable in low-concentration regimes.

evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the low covariance data.

claim: Activation of particular glomeruli may directly encode the presence of a particular odorant, or at least one among a small number of odorants with shared structural features.
source: Instead, activation of particular glomeruli may directly encode the presence of a particular odorant, or at least one among a small number of odorants with shared structural features.

claim: Sparse and selective tuning to odorant chemical features has been reported earlier for mitral/tufted cells in the mouse, using a large panel of odorants presented at approximately 1000x - 10,000x higher concentrations.
source: Notably, sparse and selective tuning to odorant chemical features has been reported earlier for mitral/tufted cells in the mouse, using a large panel of odorants presented at ~1000x - 10,000x higher concentrations (Davison and Katz, 2007; Figure 1—figure supplement 2); thus, OB circuits may maintain narrow tuning in this higher-concentration regime by suppressing the output of glomeruli that are more weakly activated by their lower affinity odorants (Yokoi et al., 1995; Gire and Schoppa, 2009; Cleland and Linster, 2012).

source: Notably, sparse and selective tuning to odorant chemical features has been reported earlier for mitral/tufted cells in the mouse, using a large panel of odorants presented at ~1000x - 10,000x higher concentrations (Davison and Katz, 2007; Figure 1—figure supplement 2); thus, OB circuits may maintain narrow tuning in this higher-concentration regime by suppressing the output of glomeruli that are more weakly activated by their lower affinity odorants (Yokoi et al., 1995; Gire and Schoppa, 2009; Cleland and Linster, 2012).

claim: Natural odors consist of mixtures of many components.
source: Natural odors consist of mixtures of many components; in a sparse coding regime, natural odors may elicit combinatorial activity patterns that directly reflect their component composition (Lin et al., 2006; Davison and Katz, 2007).

claim: In a sparse coding regime, natural odors may elicit combinatorial activity patterns that directly reflect their component composition.

claim: Despite the overall sparse representation of odorants, systematic relationships in the co-tuning of individual glomeruli to their highest-sensitivity odorants were found.

claim: Tuning of OSNs or glomeruli to shared structural features has long been noted.
source: Co-tuning relationships largely reflected straightforward features of odorant chemical structure; tuning of OSNs or glomeruli to shared structural features has long been noted (Sicard and Holley, 1984; Malnic et al., 1999; Rubin and Katz, 1999; Wachowiak and Cohen, 2001; Takahashi et al., 2004), although often these relationships have appeared complex due to the relatively broader responsiveness to a range of odorants (Saito et al., 2009; Del Mármol et al., 2021).

claim: The tuning of glomeruli to their highest-sensitivity odorants appears less complex than previously reported.

claim: Models of chemical space that incorporated a relatively small number of odorant structural features were more effective at predicting glomerular co-tuning than models generated from larger sets of computationally derived physicochemical properties.
source: Consistent with this organization, models of chemical space that incorporated a relatively small number of odorant structural features were more effective at predicting glomerular co-tuning than models generated from larger sets consisting of exhaustive lists of computationally derived physicochemical properties, and were even more effective than models based on descriptor subsets previously optimized to explain OR-odorant interactions by fitting to response data (Haddad et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to Haddad et al., 2008.

claim: Physicochemical descriptor sets have been moderately successful at predicting OR ligands and odorant perceptual attributes, but typically require careful tuning of feature selection to training datasets.
source: Physicochemical descriptor sets – which are heavily used in computational drug discovery – have been moderately successful at predicting OR ligands and odorant perceptual attributes, but typically require careful tuning of feature selection to training datasets (Boyle et al., 2013; Ravia et al., 2020; Gerkin, 2021; Kowalewski et al., 2021) and introduce hazards such as overfitting a large parameter set to a much smaller response dataset (Chae et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boyle et al., 2013; Ravia et al., 2020; Gerkin, 2021; Kowalewski et al., 2021; and Chae et al., 2019.

claim: Odorants can differ significantly from drug-like molecules in their size and other chemical features.
source: In addition, odorants can differ significantly from drug-like molecules in their size and other chemical features (Ruddigkeit et al., 2014).

claim: The SMARTS42 and MACCS fingerprints were equally or more effective at predicting the highest-sensitivity odorants for a given OSN population.
source: Thus, it is encouraging that the SMARTS42 and MACCS fingerprints used here were equally or more effective at predicting the highest-sensitivity odorants for a given OSN population, as they reflect clear substructural features of odorant molecules and required many fewer descriptors than odorants.

claim: These substructure-based models may generalize well across odorant chemical space or across different response measures.
source: These substructure-based models may generalize well across odorant chemical space or across different response measures, and could inform predictive models of odorant-OR binding (Poivet et al., 2018; Licon et al., 2019; Kowalewski and Ray, 2020) or odor perception.

source: At the same time, emphasizing the highest-sensitivity odorants for a given OSN population revealed prominent co-tuning relationships among particular odorant groups, indicating a heterogeneous structure to odorant coding space at the level of OSNs that is not adequately captured by a single set of structure-based or computationally derived chemical features.

source: The first two groups likely correspond to TAAR and class I OR glomeruli; it will be interesting to determine if the pyrazine/thiazole-tuned glomeruli reflect another distinct subfamily of ORs within the larger class II group.

claim: One implication of the heterogeneity of tuning properties is that the selectivity of different ORs may be determined by different rule sets.
source: One implication of the heterogeneity of tuning properties across the glomeruli imaged here is that the selectivity of different ORs may be determined by different rule sets.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the heterogeneity of tuning properties.

claim: Relating OR ligand binding to solved protein structures for mammalian ORs will be important in understanding the molecular basis for heterogeneity in tuning.

source: These results differ from those of earlier studies mapping chemical features across the OB surface, which used higher odorant concentrations and metabolic measures of neural activity and reported relatively discrete spatial clusters of glomeruli responsive to odorants sharing particular chemical features (Takahashi et al., 2004; Johnson and Leon, 2007).

source: Moreover, with the exception of carboxylic acid-sensitive glomeruli, which were tightly clustered within the presumed domain of class I OSN projections (Tsuboi et al., 2006; Bozza et al., 2009), spatial clustering of glomerular sensitivities was not discrete, but overlapping and interdigitated.

claim: The mosaic organization is a general feature of glomerular maps with respect to odorant chemical space.

claim: Experiments were performed using both male and female compound heterozygous crosses of OMP-IRES-tTA and tetO-GCaMP6s mice aged 2–6 months.
source: Experiments were performed using both male and female compound heterozygous crosses of OMP-IRES-tTA (Jackson Laboratory stock #017754) (Yu et al., 2004) and tetO-GCaMP6s (Jackson Laboratory stock #024742) (Wekselblatt et al., 2016) mice aged 2–6 months.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citations to Yu et al., 2004 and Wekselblatt et al., 2016.

claim: All procedures were performed following the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the University of Utah Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures were performed following the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the University of Utah Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. (IACUC protocols #19–06007, 19–06008).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Liquid dilutions of odorants were prepared to achieve target delivery concentrations of approximately 0.1, 1, 10, 100, or 1000 pM using 1:10 and 1:100 serial dilutions.
source: Liquid dilutions of odorants were prepared to achieve target delivery concentrations of approximately 0.1, 1, 10, 100, or 1000 pM (within an order-of-magnitude) using 1:10 and 1:100 serial dilutions.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Non-amine odorants were diluted in caprylic/capric medium chain triglyceride oil within approximately 1 week of experiments.
source: Non-amine odorants were diluted in caprylic/capric medium chain triglyceride oil (C3465, Spectrum Chemical Mfg. Corp.) within ~1 week of experiments; amine odorants were freshly diluted in water immediately prior to each experiment to minimize odorant oxidation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Amine odorants were freshly diluted in water immediately prior to each experiment to minimize odorant oxidation.
source: Non-amine odorants were diluted in caprylic/capric medium chain triglyceride oil (C3465, Spectrum Chemical Mfg. Corp.) within ~1 week of experiments; amine odorants were freshly diluted in water immediately prior to each experiment to minimize odorant oxidation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The OMP-IRES-tTA expression strategy did not appear to affect targeting of OSNs to their cognate glomeruli.
source: Consistent with earlier reports using the OMP-IRES-tTA driver line (Ma et al., 2014; Inagaki et al., 2020), this expression strategy did not appear to affect targeting of OSNs to their cognate glomeruli (Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2014; Inagaki et al., 2020; and Zhu et al., 2021.
